question: A choir director must select a group of singers from among his \(6\) tenors and \(8\) basses. The only requirements are that the difference between the number of tenors and basses must be a multiple of \(4,\) and the group must have at least one singer. Let \(N\) be the number of groups that can be selected. What is the remainder when \(N\) is divided by \(100?\)
solution:
Counting the basses who do not sing turns the difference condition into a condition on the size of one subset.

For a choir containing \(t\) tenors and \(b\) basses, form an auxiliary subset consisting of the selected tenors and the unselected basses. Its size is
\[
k=t+(8-b)=8+(t-b).
\]
Thus \(t-b\) is a multiple of \(4\) exactly when \(k\) is a multiple of \(4\).

This correspondence is reversible: from an auxiliary subset, select its tenors and all basses outside it. Consequently, every choir satisfying the difference condition corresponds to exactly one such subset, with no omissions or duplicates.

There are \(14\) singers, so the possible auxiliary subset sizes are \(0,4,8,12\). We must exclude the empty choir. It corresponds to the single auxiliary subset containing all eight basses and no tenors. Therefore
\[
N=\binom{14}{0}+\binom{14}{4}+\binom{14}{8}+\binom{14}{12}-1.
\]
Using \(\binom{14}{8}=\binom{14}{6}\) and \(\binom{14}{12}=\binom{14}{2}\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
N
&=1+\frac{14\cdot13\cdot12\cdot11}{4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1}
+\frac{14\cdot13\cdot12\cdot11\cdot10\cdot9}{6\cdot5\cdot4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1}
+\frac{14\cdot13}{2}-1\\
&=1+1001+3003+91-1\\
&=4095.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(4095=40\cdot100+95\), the requested remainder is \(\boxed{95}\), choice \(\text{D}\).

edges.reason: Outcome enumeration provides concrete practice partitioning and counting finite outcomes. Probability ratios are unnecessary, as Gemini notes, but that does not erase the useful enumeration component.

Dividing ordered counts by internal permutations supplies a standard derivation. Evaluating the supplied factorial quotient or a Pascal recurrence does not require first computing a permutation number.
C(n,k) evaluates an unordered selection count; the combination concept gives the object and its non-order-sensitive meaning.
The application criterion computes unordered counts by categories, containing combination-number evaluation within those categories.
edges.scope: computing unordered selection counts in applications

edges.reason: Single-valued correspondence helps formalize the encoding and its inverse. However, elementary bijective counting can work through informal one-to-one pairing without set-theoretic function language.
Congruence is defined by m dividing a-b, which presupposes knowing what a multiple is. Listing all factors is not needed, but the multiple relation itself is.
